problems.description: Session 1 introduces Celery (celery_config.py + tasks.py) with its broker/worker runtime for what is still a small auth/CRUD API — premature infrastructure that adds operational complexity unless a later story session actually consumes the task queue.
Module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, and test_api.py (5 of the 7 measured violations).
celery_config.py contains a function that is not snake_case and tasks.py contains a class that is not PascalCase (2 of the 7 measured violations).

The seed's raw-sqlite3 + Blueprint structure was replaced with Flask-SQLAlchemy + repository layer in a single greenfield session — defensible restructuring, but a large pattern departure taken in one commit rather than incrementally.

strengths: SonarQube metrics improved on every axis: smells -4, cognitive complexity -1, zero new bugs and zero duplications.
Replacing raw SQL string building with Flask-SQLAlchemy removes the SQL-injection surface and repetitive connection/dict boilerplate.
Introduces a layered structure (config, repositories, tasks) that gives later story sessions a clean seam to build on.
commit_reviews.summary: A net architectural improvement for the multi-session story — cleaner layering and better SonarQube metrics than the seed — but it carries naming-convention debt and adds Celery infrastructure that looks premature for this app's scope.

problems.description: app.config['JWT_SECRET'] falls back to the hardcoded literal 'your-secret-key-change-in-production' when the JWT_SECRET env var is unset, leaving tokens forgeable in any deployment that forgets the env var.

Schema change adds users table + tasks.owner_id FK, but db.create_all() only creates missing tables — it cannot alter the existing tasks.db from Session 1. Any pre-existing database will keep the old tasks table without owner_id and error at runtime; no migration path is added.

All auth (User model, token_required, register/login) is bolted into single-file app.py alongside CRUD, growing cognitive complexity +22 and adding 3 smells in one session; no modularization despite the surface area increase.
No password policy (minimum length/complexity) on register; empty strings are the only rejection, so trivial passwords are accepted and hashed.

Auth register/login tests are added, but the visible test diff does not cover cross-user ownership isolation (that user A cannot read/update/delete user B's tasks) — the core invariant this session introduces.

strengths: Every task query filters by owner_id (create/get/update/list), so per-user ownership scoping is enforced server-side with no IDOR gaps.
Passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never stored or returned plaintext.
JWT issued with a 24h expiry and HS256 pinned explicitly; token_required handles missing/malformed/expired tokens cleanly.
Composite unique constraint (title, owner_id) preserves per-user title uniqueness without breaking cross-user duplicates.
Tests added for auth flows using small helper functions and the existing fixture pattern; error responses consistently use the established jsonify shape.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, natural story progression that adds JWT auth and correct per-user task scoping with hashed passwords and new tests — but introduces real technical debt via a hardcoded JWT secret fallback and a schema change with no migration for pre-existing databases, and the measured 0.77 convention score is polluted by violations in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py) plus a stale app.py UPPER_CASE flag that does not match the actual diff content.

problems.description: app.py:60 — import of repositories is placed mid-file after db.create_all(); works around the import order but reads as a code smell and can mask circular-dependency issues.
repositories.py — get_by_id(self, id) shadows the builtin id; parameter and attribute naming is inconsistent (model stored twice as self.model and self.User).
repositories.py — exists_by_username fetches the full User row via filter_by().first() just to test existence; a scalar/exists query would avoid materializing the entity.
repositories.py — BaseRepository.update() is dead code; app.py still mutates attributes directly and calls commit(), so the abstraction is not fully adopted.
repositories.py — access patterns are inconsistent within the layer: get_by_id uses db.session.get while exists/get_by_* use model.query.filter_by.

strengths: Cohesive repository layer that centralizes data access and removes repeated filter_by/add/commit/rollback boilerplate across routes
Consistent error handling preserved: every transactional path keeps its rollback on exception
No behavioral change to endpoints; token ownership scoping (get_by_id_and_owner) is correctly maintained
Correct use of db.session.get for primary-key lookups
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-scoped repository-pattern refactor that reduces route duplication and preserves behavior, with only minor nits (mid-file import, shadowed builtin, full-object existence check, dead update() method) and no meaningful new debt — the 0.77 convention score is dragged down by violations in files this commit barely touches (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_api.py), which is a discrepancy worth flagging.

problems.description: Cursor pagination loads the full task list via get_all_by_owner() and slices in Python, so every page is O(n) in memory/time — a faux keyset pagination that adds complexity (+31 cognitive complexity) without scaling; a real implementation would be a SQL WHERE id > cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT n.

Bare `except:` in get_rate_limit_key() swallows all exceptions (JWT decode errors, IndexError, KeyError) and silently falls through to the IP key — should catch jwt.InvalidTokenError/IndexError explicitly.

The '100 per minute' literal is duplicated in the Limiter() constructor and all 5 route decorators; it should be a single module-level UPPER_CASE constant (which also resolves the app.py module-constant convention violation).

Redundant rate limiting: identical @limiter.limit('100 per minute') per route is applied on top of default_limits=['100 per minute'], so each route carries two equivalent rules — one mechanism or the other.

client and client_with_rate_limit fixtures both mutate shared module-level app state (limiter.enabled, app.config['TESTING']) with only partial reset in the plain fixture — fragile if test order or parallelism changes.

GET /tasks response shape changes from a bare list to an envelope (data/next_cursor/total) — a backward-incompatible contract break with no versioning; acceptable for the demo app since all tests were updated coherently.

strengths: Well-tested cross-cutting work: dedicated rate-limit fixture that cleanly skips when Redis is unavailable and resets state (flushdb, limiter re-disable) in a finally block.
429 handler returns a JSON error shape consistent with the app's existing error conventions.
JWT-aware rate-limit key gives per-user buckets with a sensible IP fallback for anonymous requests.
Pagination envelope (data/next_cursor/total) with limit clamping to 1-100 is coherent and all existing assertions were updated to match.

Respects existing patterns: repository layer, decorator-based auth, env-var config, error-handler style — only app.py and test_api.py are touched, and 5 of the 7 flagged convention violations are pre-existing in files untouched by this diff.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid cross-cutting session (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that fits the story's architecture and is well-tested, but the pagination is an in-memory slice rather than a true keyset query and minor convention/debt items (bare except, duplicated limit literal, redundant per-route limits) keep it from being clean — qualitative judgment agrees with the 0.77 mechanical convention score.

compounding_issues: Session 1's flat-file JSON store with an in-process threading.Lock was never upgraded to a database; reads (get_tasks/get_task) are unlocked and the lock is process-local, so the Celery worker introduced in session 3 can race the Flask process on tasks.json writes
Session 2's legacy-data migration created a 'legacy' user with a hardcoded known password_hash('legacy') that persists through sessions 3-5 as an auth backdoor
Session 3's Celery integration made Redis a hard runtime dependency (broker/result backend + session 5's rate-limiter storage), so the app no longer runs standalone without infrastructure
The monotonic app.py growth (121 -> 285 -> 297 lines) before the session-4 refactor meant feature sessions 2-3 carried accumulating single-file complexity until the debt was explicitly paid down
key_decisions: Session 1: swap the SQLite seed for JSON flat-file storage under a threading lock to honor the 'no databases' constraint
Session 2: introduce JWT auth, a user model, and owner-scoped tasks, shifting the app from single-user todo to multi-tenant model with a legacy-data migration
Session 3: add Celery + Redis async email notifications, establishing an async side-channel and making Redis a first-class dependency
Session 4: extract a repositories.py data-access layer (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository), slimming app.py from ~297 to ~200 lines
Session 5: add Flask-Limiter rate limiting keyed per authenticated user plus owner-scoped pagination, building directly on the session-4 repository layer
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. The test suite grew 10 -> 24 -> 32 -> 32 -> 50 passing tests with zero regressions, and the codebase evolved from a 121-line single-file monolith (session 1) through feature additions (auth in 2, async notifications in 3) to a deliberately layered structure after the session-4 repository extraction, which paid off immediately when session 5 layered rate limiting and pagination onto the clean data-access seam. The only structural wobble was pre-refactor app.py bloat (285-297 lines) that the session-4 refactor corrected, leaving HEAD at 275-line app.py plus dedicated repositories/celery/config modules with all 50 tests passing.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, textbook progression — greenfield storage choice, multi-user auth, async integration, repository-layer refactor, then cross-cutting concerns — where each session built on the prior one and the session-4 refactor turned accumulated single-file debt into a seam that made session 5 land cleanly, at the cost of a persistent legacy-user backdoor and process-local locking that never fully matched the async worker model.
